extracted.intended_audience: educational institutions (K-12 and postsecondary), Title IX coordinators, school administrators, campus officials, and institutional legal counsel/policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: Preamble to the Department of Education's final Title IX regulations describing definitions of sexual harassment, notice/actual-knowledge standards, reporting and investigative obligations, and institutional duties for K-12 and postsecondary recipients of federal funds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Sexual Harassment (unwelcome conduct on the basis of sex)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 106.30 provides that 'sexual harassment' is conduct 'on the basis of sex' including 'unwelcome conduct.' The final regulations continue the 1997/2001 approach of including unwelcome sexual advances, requests for sexual favors, and other verbal, nonverbal, or physical conduct of a sexual nature by an employee, by another student, or by a third party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the foundational definitional criterion: sexual harassment is sex-based unwelcome conduct. The regulation also expressly recognizes sex-based violence as sexual harassment and ties definitions to Clery Act/VAWA offenses where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Davis definition verbatim (severe, pervasive, and objectively offensive)
rubrics_metrics.description: One category of conduct that constitutes sexual harassment uses the Davis Court's phrasing verbatim: unwelcome conduct that a reasonable person would determine is 'so severe, pervasive, and objectively offensive' that it effectively denies a person equal access to education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department returns to the Davis formulation to provide consistency between judicial and administrative enforcement; this phrasing is used as one of three categories of actionable sexual harassment under the final regs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of Clery Act/VAWA offenses as sexual harassment (single-instance coverage)
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations incorporate sexual assault as defined in the Clery Act and also incorporate the definitions of dating violence, domestic violence, and stalking (as amended by VAWA) into §106.30, clarifying that sexual harassment includes a single instance of sexual assault, dating violence, domestic violence, or stalking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By including these offenses without requiring them to meet Davis elements (severity/pervasiveness/objective offensiveness), the regs avoid cases where some sex offenses would be excluded as 'not pervasive' and provide clarity at the intersection of Title IX, the Clery Act, and VAWA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retention of quid pro quo harassment
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations retain the proposed rules' definition of 'quid pro quo' harassment in the definition of sexual harassment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quid pro quo harassment remains explicitly recognized (as it had been in 1997 and 2001 guidance and related case law) as one form of sexual harassment requiring a recipient response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency and simplicity of a single, uniform definition
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department emphasizes returning to the premise that a consistent definition used in both judicial and administrative enforcement is appropriate: 'The Department has an interest in providing recipients with "consistency and simplicity in understanding what is sexual harassment for which the school must take responsive action. A multiplicity of definitions would not serve this purpose."'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoids having separate definitions for private lawsuits and administrative enforcement to reduce uncertainty and confusion for recipients, students, and employees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients may address non-Title IX harassing conduct under other provisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Dismissal of a formal complaint because the allegations do not meet the Title IX definition of sexual harassment does not preclude a recipient from addressing the alleged misconduct under other provisions of the recipient's own code of conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions retain authority to discipline or address conduct outside the scope of Title IX via their own codes; §106.45(b)(3)(i) was changed to clarify this point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actual knowledge condition adopted and adapted
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department adopts and adapts the Gebser/Davis framework's condition of 'actual knowledge' as the trigger for when a recipient's own intentional discrimination can be found.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The regs prohibit a recipient's own intentional discrimination but adapt the actual-knowledge concept to administrative enforcement needs (e.g., broaden who counts as providing notice) rather than adopting constructive notice or vicarious liability theories used in prior guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who conveys actual knowledge: Title IX Coordinator or officials with authority
rubrics_metrics.description: For all recipients, notice to the recipient's Title IX Coordinator or to 'any official of the recipient who has authority to institute corrective measures on behalf of the recipient' (referred to as 'officials with authority') conveys actual knowledge to the recipient and triggers the recipient's response obligations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether an individual is an 'official with authority' is a legal, fact-specific determination based on the recipient's administrative structure and roles. Notice to these individuals is treated as notice to the institution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elementary and secondary standard: notice to any employee triggers response
rubrics_metrics.description: In elementary and secondary schools, notice to 'any employee' (in addition to notice to the Title IX Coordinator or to any official with authority) triggers the recipient's response obligations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because elementary/secondary employees exercise control/supervision and often are mandatory reporters under state law, requiring response upon notice to any employee furthers Title IX objectives and avoids expecting young students to distinguish among employee roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Postsecondary standard: notice to Title IX Coordinator or official with authority triggers response
rubrics_metrics.description: In postsecondary institutions, where in loco parentis does not apply, notice to the Title IX Coordinator or any official with authority conveys actual knowledge to the recipient and triggers the recipient's obligations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach respects complainant autonomy at colleges/universities by allowing institutions to decide which employees must/may report to the Coordinator, preserving the option for confidential disclosures to some employees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Departure from 'responsible employees' rubric and 'should have known' constructive notice
rubrics_metrics.description: These final regulations do not use the 'responsible employees' rubric from guidance and depart from the constructive notice condition that triggered responses when a recipient's responsible employees 'should have known' about harassment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The regulations discard the 'should have known' standard because it was vague, led to wide-net mandatory-reporting policies, and could produce privacy-invasive inquiries; instead, the regs set clearer, administrable triggers for response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to investigate when a formal complaint is filed or signed by Title IX Coordinator
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations clearly obligate a recipient to investigate and adjudicate whenever a complainant files, or a Title IX Coordinator signs, a formal complaint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department will hold recipients responsible for failure or refusal to investigate a formal complaint. The regs do not require speculation about what an investigation would have revealed (rejecting prior 'should have known' hypotheticals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear reporting channels and notice of Title IX Coordinator contact information
rubrics_metrics.description: These final regulations ensure that all students and employees are notified of the contact information for the Title IX Coordinator and how to report sexual harassment; any person may always trigger a recipient's response obligations by reporting sexual harassment to the Title IX Coordinator using posted contact information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporting options must include accessible channels (including during non-business hours). The person who reports need not be the complainant; reports may be made by 'any person' who believes harassment may have occurred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Postsecondary discretion on mandatory reporters vs confidential resources
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations allow postsecondary institutions wide discretion to craft and implement their own employee reporting policy to decide which employees are mandatory reporters (must report), which employees may keep disclosures confidential (may listen without reporting), and which employees must report only with the complainant's consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This permits institutions to balance respecting complainant autonomy and access to supportive measures while still ensuring clear reporting channels to trigger institutional responses when desired by complainants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training/ability/obligation to report alone does not make someone an official with authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere ability or obligation to report sexual harassment, or having been trained to do so, does not qualify an individual (such as a volunteer parent, or alumnus) as an official with authority to institute corrective measures on behalf of the recipient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department will not assume that a person is an official with authority solely because they received training or have the ability/obligation to report; this avoids discouraging training and clarifies the narrowness of the 'official with authority' concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy objectives guiding the regulatory choices
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department's adaptions of the Gebser/Davis framework aim to further Title IX purposes in administrative enforcement by: respecting freedom of speech and academic freedom; respecting complainants' autonomy; protecting complainants' equal educational access while respecting State/local determinations of supportive measures and sanctions; ensuring consistency with constitutional due process and fundamental fairness; and providing clear legal obligations to enable robust administrative enforcement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These articulated policy objectives frame definitional and procedural choices (e.g., returning to Davis wording, including Clery/VAWA offenses, tailoring notice triggers by educational level) and serve as evaluative criteria for whether the regs appropriately balance competing interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptation to hold recipients responsible for broader actions than Gebser/Davis required
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department adapts the three-part Gebser/Davis framework 'to further the purposes of Title IX in the context of administrative enforcement, holding schools responsible for taking more actions than what the Gebser/Davis framework requires.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the regs adopt Gebser/Davis' actual knowledge threshold, they modify who qualifies as providing notice and other mechanics so administrative enforcement leads to more proactive institutional responses consistent with Title IX aims.
